## M3-E02

**Let SQLite choose the primary key** · SOURCE · demonstrated in the lecture  
Source: [lecture3 L206-232](../sources/lecture3.txt) *“So it seems like SQLite actually increments the primary key for me.”*

```sql
INSERT INTO "collections" ("title", "accession_number", "acquired")
VALUES ('Spring Outing', '14.76', '1914-01-08');
```

**Why:** SQLite takes the current highest id (2) and adds 1, giving 3. Choosing ids yourself risks reusing one that is already taken.
For what changes with `AUTOINCREMENT`, see errata #2: the lecture states it backwards.

<details><summary>Expected output</summary>

After your SQL, the checker runs:

`SELECT * FROM "collections"`

| id | title | accession_number | acquired |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Profusion of Flowers | 56.257 | 1956-04-12 |
| 2 | Farmers Working at Dawn | 11.6152 | 1911-08-03 |
| 3 | Spring Outing | 14.76 | 1914-01-08 |

</details>

## M3-E05

**Insert two rows in one statement** · SOURCE · demonstrated in the lecture  
Source: [lecture3 L334-364](../sources/lecture3.txt) *“So a handy way to insert more than one value.”*

```sql
INSERT INTO "collections" ("title", "accession_number", "acquired")
VALUES
('Imaginative Landscape', '56.496', NULL),
('Peonies and Butterfly', '06.1899', '1906-01-01');
```

**Why:** One multi-row INSERT is both more convenient and faster than many single inserts. It is also all-or-nothing:
if one row violates a constraint, none are inserted (L632-638).

<details><summary>Expected output</summary>

After your SQL, the checker runs:

`SELECT "title", "accession_number", "acquired" FROM "collections"`

| title | accession_number | acquired |
|---|---|---|
| Profusion of Flowers | 56.257 | 1956-04-12 |
| Farmers Working at Dawn | 11.6152 | 1911-08-03 |
| Spring Outing | 14.76 | 1914-01-08 |
| Imaginative Landscape | 56.496 | NULL |
| Peonies and Butterfly | 06.1899 | 1906-01-01 |

</details>

## M3-E06

**From an imported CSV into the real table** · SOURCE · demonstrated in the lecture  
Source: [lecture3 L570-603](../sources/lecture3.txt) *“I actually have a way to dynamically select all the values I want to insert”*, [lecture3 L644-663](../sources/lecture3.txt) *“it won't be converted to”*

```sql
INSERT INTO "collections" ("title", "accession_number", "acquired")
SELECT "title", "accession_number", NULLIF("acquired", '') FROM "temp";
DROP TABLE "temp";
```

**Why:** The lecture moves the rows with `INSERT INTO ... SELECT` (L570-595) and notes that CSV blanks import as empty text, not NULL (L640-663).
`NULLIF` is one way to do the clean-up it recommends. The lecture suggests a later UPDATE instead, and either works.

## M3-E09

**Delete an artist the two-step way** · SOURCE · demonstrated in the lecture  
Source: [lecture3 L954-979](../sources/lecture3.txt) *“First delete their affiliation, then delete their name.”*

```sql

    SELECT "id" FROM "artists" WHERE "name" = 'Unidentified artist'
```

## M3-E10

**Hit the FOREIGN KEY constraint** · SOURCE · demonstrated in the lecture  
Source: [lecture3 L885-896](../sources/lecture3.txt) *“I do get that FOREIGN KEY constraint error”*

```sql
DELETE FROM "artists" WHERE "name" = 'Unidentified artist';
```

**Why:** The default action is effectively RESTRICT. SQLite refuses to leave `created` pointing at nothing.
(This only happens with `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON`.)

<details><summary>Expected output</summary>

The statement must fail with:
```text
FOREIGN KEY constraint failed
```

</details>

## M3-E11

**Let ON DELETE CASCADE do both steps** · SOURCE · demonstrated in the lecture  
Source: [lecture3 L988-1013](../sources/lecture3.txt) *“This converts our 2-step process into a 1-step process.”*, [lecture3 L1044-1052](../sources/lecture3.txt) *“I've also deleted the artist's affiliation with their work”*

```sql

```

**Why:** The other ON DELETE choices: RESTRICT (refuse), NO ACTION (allow, leaving dangling ids), SET NULL, SET DEFAULT, and CASCADE.

## M3-E13

**Clean the votes and get four groups** · SOURCE · demonstrated in the lecture  
Source: [lecture3 L1281-1299](../sources/lecture3.txt) *“takes a string and just removes leading and trailing”*, [lecture3 L1384-1394](../sources/lecture3.txt) *“so be careful with this”*, [lecture3 L1444-1448](../sources/lecture3.txt) *“Farmers Working At Dawn has six votes.”*

```sql
UPDATE "votes" SET "title" = trim("title");
UPDATE "votes" SET "title" = upper("title");
UPDATE "votes" SET "title" = 'FARMERS WORKING AT DAWN' WHERE "title" LIKE 'Fa%';
UPDATE "votes" SET "title" = 'IMAGINATIVE LANDSCAPE' WHERE "title" LIKE 'Imaginative %';
UPDATE "votes" SET "title" = 'IMAGINATIVE LANDSCAPE' WHERE "title" = 'IMAGINTIVE LANDSCAPE';
UPDATE "votes" SET "title" = 'PROFUSION OF FLOWERS' WHERE "title" LIKE 'Profusion%';
```

**Why:** The final tally is Farmers 6, Imaginative 5, Profusion 5, Spring Outing 4. The lecture reports 6 and 5 for the first two.
`LIKE 'Fa%'` is fine for this tiny data set, but in real data it could also match other titles (see debugging D3-06).

<details><summary>Expected output</summary>

After your SQL, the checker runs:

`SELECT upper("title"), COUNT(*) FROM "votes" GROUP BY upper("title")`

| upper("title") | COUNT(*) |
|---|---|
| FARMERS WORKING AT DAWN | 6 |
| IMAGINATIVE LANDSCAPE | 5 |
| PROFUSION OF FLOWERS | 5 |
| SPRING OUTING | 4 |

`SELECT COUNT(*) FROM "votes" WHERE "title" != trim("title")`

| COUNT(*) |
|---|
| 0 |

</details>

## M3-E14

**Triggers that log sales and purchases** · SOURCE · demonstrated in the lecture  
Source: [lecture3 L1588-1631](../sources/lecture3.txt) *“So automatically, I added "Profusion of Flowers"”*, [lecture3 L1638-1678](../sources/lecture3.txt) *“So this is the power of triggers.”*

```sql
CREATE TABLE "transactions" (
    "id" INTEGER,
    "title" TEXT,
    "action" TEXT,
    PRIMARY KEY("id")
);
CREATE TRIGGER "sell"
BEFORE DELETE ON "collections"
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
    INSERT INTO "transactions" ("title", "action")
    VALUES (OLD."title", 'sold');
END;
CREATE TRIGGER "buy"
AFTER INSERT ON "collections"
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
    INSERT INTO "transactions" ("title", "action")
    VALUES (NEW."title", 'bought');
END;
```

**Why:** You never typed an INSERT into `transactions`. The triggers ran it for you. `FOR EACH ROW` means a DELETE of 3 rows logs 3 sales.

<details><summary>Expected output</summary>

After your SQL, the checker runs:

`SELECT "title", "action" FROM "transactions" ORDER BY "id"`

| title | action |
|---|---|

_(no rows)_

</details>

## M3-E15

**Soft-delete instead of delete** · SOURCE · demonstrated in the lecture  
Source: [lecture3 L1737-1757](../sources/lecture3.txt) *“but technically-- at least we marked it as deleted”*

```sql
ALTER TABLE "collections" ADD COLUMN "deleted" INTEGER DEFAULT 0;
UPDATE "collections" SET "deleted" = 1 WHERE "title" = 'Farmers Working at Dawn';
```

**Why:** Now every query must filter on `"deleted" = 0` (or `!= 1`), which is why Lecture 4 wraps that filter in a view.
Ethics: for personal data, a soft delete may not honour a request to be forgotten (GDPR, L1774-1784).

<details><summary>Expected output</summary>

After your SQL, the checker runs:

`SELECT "title", "deleted" FROM "collections"`

| title | deleted |
|---|---|
| Farmers Working at Dawn | 1 |
| Imaginative Landscape | 0 |
| Profusion of Flowers | 0 |
| Spring Outing | 0 |

</details>

## D3-05

**NEW in a DELETE trigger** · GENERATED · written for this system (reinforces a concept from the source)  
Source: [lecture3 L1603-1608](../sources/lecture3.txt) *“you get access to this keyword called old”*

Broken version:
```sql
CREATE TRIGGER "sell" BEFORE DELETE ON "collections"
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
    INSERT INTO "transactions" ("title", "action") VALUES (NEW."title", 'sold');
END;
```

Fixed:
```sql
CREATE TRIGGER "sell" BEFORE DELETE ON "collections"
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
    INSERT INTO "transactions" ("title", "action") VALUES (OLD."title", 'sold');
END;
```

**Diagnosis (trigger):** `OLD` is the row being removed. `NEW` only exists for INSERT and UPDATE.
SQLite does not check this when you create the trigger. The error (`no such column: NEW.title`) appears only when the trigger fires.

<details><summary>Expected output</summary>

After your SQL, the checker runs:

`SELECT "title", "action" FROM "transactions"`

| title | action |
|---|---|

_(no rows)_

</details>

## D3-06

**An over-eager LIKE** · SOURCE · question posed in the lecture  
Source: [lecture3 L1388-1394](../sources/lecture3.txt) *“because you could match much more than Farmers Working At Dawn”*

Broken version:
```sql
UPDATE "votes" SET "title" = 'Farmers Working at Dawn' WHERE "title" LIKE 'Fa%';
```

Fixed:
```sql
UPDATE "votes" SET "title" = 'Farmers Working at Dawn'
WHERE "title" LIKE 'Farm%' OR "title" LIKE 'Fame%';
```
